title: Old vines
subtitle: Living history
objectives: Explain why the Barossa has old vines

steps.title: Phylloxera-free
steps.body: South Australia has never had phylloxera, thanks to strict quarantine laws. So the Barossa has some of the world's oldest producing vines, ungrafted, on their own roots. Some Shiraz vines were planted in the 1840s, like at Langmeil's Freedom vineyard and Turkey Flat; Grenache and Mourvèdre vines are similarly old.

steps.title: The Old Vine Charter
steps.body: In 2009, the Barossa created the Old Vine Charter to register and protect old vineyards. It has four levels: Old Vine, at least 35 years; Survivor Vine, 70 years; Centenarian Vine, 100 years; and Ancestor Vine, 125 years or more. Producers can show these on labels.

steps.prompt: Order the Barossa Old Vine Charter levels from youngest to oldest.

steps.title: Why they matter
steps.body: Old vines have deep roots that find water in drought, so many are dry-grown. They give low yields of small, concentrated berries, with balance and complexity. They're also a living record of 19th century viticulture, and valuable genetic material, since Europe's original vines were mostly lost to phylloxera.

steps.prompt: Why does the Barossa have such old vines?

steps.title: What you learned
points: South Australia is phylloxera-free, so old vines survive
The Old Vine Charter registers vines from 35 to 125 years
Old vines give low, concentrated yields and living history
